title: The great freeze
text: Gondwana lies over the South Pole. Almost all life is in the sea. Ice sheets grow across the polar land. So much water is locked up that the sea falls. The warm, shallow seas where most animals live drain away or turn cold. Then the ice melts. Water low in oxygen spreads across the sea floor — a second wave of death. About 85% of sea species are gone.
prompt:
A painting for a natural-history museum: The great freeze, about 444 million years ago.
Painted in the manner of Charles R. Knight (1874–1953), the American natural-history muralist: oil on canvas, confident visible brushwork, warm golden naturalistic light, soft atmospheric haze, a palette of ochres, siennas, olive greens and dusty blues, calm and dignified realism. Keep his warmth and his eye for the real world, but follow TODAY's science, not the science of his time: paint the land, water, plants and climate exactly as described here.
What happened, from the scientific evidence: Gondwana lies over the South Pole. Almost all life is in the sea. Ice sheets grow across the polar land. So much water is locked up that the sea falls. The warm, shallow seas where most animals live drain away or turn cold. Then the ice melts. Water low in oxygen spreads across the sea floor — a second wave of death. About 85% of sea species are gone.
Paint the moment as seen from high in the sky: a wide view of the land and sea where it happened, as they were THEN — the continents, coasts, plants and life of that time, not today's. Show only what the description says. Living things only where it names them, small, as they are reconstructed today; none where it does not.
What could not yet exist then, so must not be painted: NO trees, shrubs or bushes: the only land plants are tiny, low, moss-like plants a few centimetres tall, near water.
No text, labels, map lines, arrows, borders or frame.
